tagline.text: Quiet white sand and cave pools at Bohol's eastern edge

children.text: A quiet coastal town on a peninsula jutting from Bohol Island's eastern edge, prized for the fine white sand of Quinale Beach and clear cave pools in the limestone terrain. Far quieter than Panglao, it suits travelers wanting an unhurried rest and diving.
Anda is a small coastal town of roughly 20,000 people on a blunt peninsula at the southeastern tip of Bohol Island. At
2.5–3 hours
by car from Tagbilaran or Panglao, it long remained a beach known only to locals, but more recently travelers and divers looking to escape Panglao's crowds have quietly begun coming here.
Anda's coastline is a series of small bays and headlands, each hiding flour-fine white sand beaches. Quinale Beach, at the heart of the town, is a public beach stretching nearly
1km
, with clear water and gentle waves right offshore, good for family swims. Facing east, it also offers sunrise views over the sea, unlike west-coast-centered Panglao.

The whole peninsula sits on limestone terrain riddled with underground-water caves, some of which have open ceilings that let sunlight in, forming natural pools. The best known, Cabagnow Cave Pool, is a blue pool

deep, famous for jumping in from above. On the peninsula's east coast at Lamanok, ancient rock art painted in red pigment and old burial caves remain, offering a glimpse of Bohol's prehistoric inhabitants.

Anda's offshore waters meet the deep Bohol Sea, giving rise to several dive sites rich in sheer coral walls and macro life. With almost no large resorts or nightlife, it suits a style of travel built around renting a motorbike and seeking out beaches, caves, and waterfalls one by one — especially well suited to couples wanting quiet rest, long-term travelers, and divers.

blocks.title: Swimming and sunrise at Quinale Beach

children.text: The public beach at the heart of Anda has no entrance fee and features fine white sand and calm water. Watching the sun rise over the sea from the beach in the early morning is Anda's signature experience.
A cave pool where a blue underground-water pool opens up below a narrow rock crevice, letting you jump into water about
deep. You can also enter slowly via an iron ladder; it has designated rest days for conservation, so check before visiting.
Beyond Cabagnow, the peninsula has cave pools of varying scale and atmosphere, such as Kaligoon Cave Pool. You can visit two or three by motorbike in half a day.

On Lamanok Island, a small island off the village of Badiang on the northeast of the peninsula, you follow a local guide past mangroves and rock cliffs to see red handprints, ancient human-shaped murals, and old burial caves.

The sheer coral walls and sloping sites close offshore are rich with fan corals, turtles, and small creatures like cowries and nudibranchs. Currents are generally mild, making it good for beginner divers too.

blocks.title: Can-Umantad Falls and its rice terraces

children.text: Can-Umantad Falls in neighboring Candijay is one of Bohol's largest waterfalls, with the Cadapdapan rice terraces spreading out above it. It's about
30–40 minutes
from Anda by car.
The coastal road circling the Anda peninsula runs past emerald water and small hidden beaches. Pulling over to rest at an unnamed beach is part of the charm of touring this area by motorbike.

, and large luggage may be charged as an extra seat. The road follows the coast through several villages, so it takes time but the scenery is good. Services thin out in the late afternoon, so we recommend leaving in the morning.
If you took a boat from Camiguin Island in Mindanao and landed at Jagna Port in southern Bohol, it takes about
1 hour
from Jagna to Anda by bus or van, at around
. It is much closer than going through Tagbilaran.
Chartering a car from Panglao or the airport to Anda costs about
one way. It's efficient to combine it into a day tour that also stops at the Loboc River or the Chocolate Hills along the way.
Within Anda, renting a motorbike (about
a day) is most convenient, and chartering a tricycle or habal-habal (about
for half a day) is also an option.
Anda faces east, so it's affected by the northeast monsoon. During
December–February
, windy days can bring waves and drifting seaweed to the beach, so
March–May
, when the sea is calmest and clearest, is the best time. Sunrises are also sharpest and diving visibility best during this period.
June–November

is the rainy season with frequent showers, but the sea isn't always rough on many days, so travel is still feasible. That said, cave pools can turn cloudy after heavy rain, and Can-Umantad Falls gains more force from higher water volume but the access road turns muddy. When a typhoon or tropical depression affects the area during
October–December
, the coastal road and diving plans can be disrupted.
During Holy Week and the
May
holidays, local Bohol residents crowd Quinale Beach and weekend afternoons get busy, but on weekdays you can have the beach almost to yourself.

Accommodations are scattered around Quinale Beach and along the coast west of town. Beachfront boutique resorts run about
a night, dive resorts and mid-range lodging run about
, and village guesthouses run about
. Since resorts are spread apart and hard to walk between, it's worth also weighing restaurant and beach access when choosing where to stay.

With few restaurants around, most meals end up being at your resort's restaurant. Around the town-center market and beach area, carinderias sell grilled fish and Filipino home cooking, so you can get a meal for about
. As a coastal town, the day's catch of fish and squid, and kinilaw, are fresh, and snacks made from locally grown mango and banana are also worth trying.
There is one Metrobank ATM at the entrance to Anda's town hall that accepts foreign cards, but it dispenses only up to
at a time, charges a fee, and often breaks down or runs out of cash. Bring plenty of the cash you need from Tagbilaran or Panglao. Many small resorts do not accept card payments.
Cave pools have set closing days and opening hours by day of the week. Confirm through your accommodation or local tourism info before planning your itinerary.
Cabagnow Cave Pool is generally open
8:00 AM to 3:30 PM
, and swimming is not allowed on Mondays and Fridays. Admission is about
, plus a separate
environmental fee; if you've already paid the environmental fee elsewhere in Anda, show your receipt and you won't have to pay it again.
Cave pool rocks are very slippery. Wear aqua shoes, and confirm the water depth and rock positions with staff before jumping in.
Watch for sharp curves and slopes on the coastal road when riding a motorbike, and get back to your accommodation before dark.
Smart and Globe signal reaches the town center but is weak along the outer coast and around the caves. Download offline maps in advance.
Good photo spots are the Quinale Beach sunrise, a view looking down into Cabagnow Cave Pool, and the rice terraces above Can-Umantad Falls.

At cave pool jump points, always go one person at a time, confirming the person below has cleared the area before jumping. The water is deep, but accidents can still happen from hitting the edge rocks.
At the cave pools and the Lamanok rock art site, don't touch the rock paintings or stalactites, and the rule is not to enter wearing soap or sunscreen.
There are sea urchins and sharp coral just offshore. Don't walk barefoot at low tide.
Anda has no major hospital. Serious injuries or illness require traveling to Tagbilaran, so bring basic medication.
After heavy rain in the rainy season, the current around the waterfall picks up sharply. Don't swim in areas staff have designated off-limits.
